remarks: For pre-construction cases, the Fire Department issues a provisional Fire NOC based on blueprints; the final Fire NOC is issued after completion and verification of safety installations.

findings.text: The Fire NOC service is currently offline; applications are submitted physically to the concerned Officer-in-Charge and the final NOC is collected physically.
A dedicated Fire Safety NOC portal has been fully designed and is in final testing, with the department planning to move fully online, probably within 2026 or early 2027.
Applicants generally make two office visits (to submit the form and to receive the final NOC), with additional visits sometimes needed to enquire about status.
Physical inspection and verification, including completion of the checklist/field report, was identified as the most time-consuming stage, depending on occupancy and compliance.

Inspection is based on occupancy and hazard classification (low, moderate, high) following the National Building Code of India, with occupancy-specific checklists for categories such as educational, residential and industrial buildings.
No application, approval or other official fee is currently levied for Fire Safety NOC.
A committee has proposed license fees for Fire NOC based on building floor area; the proposal was submitted to the Government and approval was awaited at the time of discussion.
There is no deemed-approval provision for Fire NOC.
Physical inspection is the most challenging activity for the department because officers must physically travel to and inspect the site.
Manual data maintenance in the offline system means records pile up after NOC issuance, making it difficult at times to track and notify owners about the expiry of the three-year NOC.
Implement geotagged photographs as part of verification, retaining necessary physical verification for safety.
Implement planned SMS/email notifications for application status, reasons for rejection/approval and renewal/expiry alerts.
Consider API integration or a hyperlink with the State Single Window System once the departmental portal is operational.

The department formulated its own Fire Safety checklist in 2022 after reviewing practices in states such as Tamil Nadu and Kerala, adapted for Nagaland's hilly terrain and in adherence to the National Building Code of India.
Self-declaration and video verification were discussed as possible alternatives, but the experts were not certain about their use as replacements for physical inspection.
The application format is incorporated in the Nagaland Fire and Emergency Services Act, 2021, while the inspection checklist is Government-approved but not reflected in the Act.

gaps.text: No average end-to-end time from initial application to final Fire NOC was given; only the post-inspection, one-month FHQ processing stage is specified.
The department had no data on the total number of applications received, approved/disposed or pending; only that 126 Fire NOCs were issued in FY 2025-26.
A fee proposal based on building floor area has been submitted to the Government, but the proposed amounts and approval status were not resolved at the time of discussion.
A dedicated Fire Safety NOC portal is fully designed and in final testing, expected to replace the current offline process, probably within 2026 or early 2027.
The department's own Fire Safety checklist, developed in 2022 drawing on Tamil Nadu and Kerala practice and adapted for Nagaland's hilly terrain, in line with the National Building Code.

timeline.text: This is a recurring compliance filing, not a one-time approval process. Monthly regular filers file GSTR-1 by the 11th and GSTR-3B by the 20th of the subsequent month; Composition Scheme filers file CMP-08 quarterly; QRMP filers file GSTR-1 monthly or quarterly and GSTR-3B quarterly. No departmental resolution timeline for flagged discrepancies was mentioned.

fees.text: No filing application fee or official statutory filing fee was specifically mentioned. Late fees for delayed filing: ₹20 per day for Nil filers (₹10 under CGST and ₹10 under SGST), capped at ₹500 per month; ₹50 per day for Non-Nil filers, capped at ₹2,000 for a particular month. For tax paid in cash after the 20th, 18% per annum interest is auto-calculated by the system and added to the next GSTR-3B; local officers have no discretionary power to waive these system-imposed late fees and interest manually.

remarks: GST processes are broadly all-India in nature; the expert stated there is nothing Nagaland-specific in the process described.
The process became easier after second-generation reforms referred to as GST 2.0, implemented from 25 September 2025.
The Tax Office is present to enforce the Act, not to file returns on behalf of taxpayers; officials guide and train taxpayers who want to file themselves.

Some agencies may insist on a GST registration number for government schemes or bank loans, leading some people to obtain GST numbers without taxable turnover, not file returns, and later face penalties.
Businesses must maintain books of accounts for 60 months under Sections 35 and 36, as cited by the expert.

findings.text: The process became easier after GST 2.0 (second-generation reforms), implemented from 25 September 2025.
90% to 95% of dealers in Kohima hire local accountants, Chartered Accountants or certified GST Practitioners, as many small traders are not tech-savvy and consultants manage monthly filings.
Peak system traffic occurs near filing deadlines, particularly the 18th to 20th, and local network issues affect remote areas.
Late fees are ₹20/day for Nil filers (capped at ₹500/month) and ₹50/day for Non-Nil filers (capped at ₹2,000/month).

18% per annum interest is auto-calculated on cash tax paid after the 20th and added to the next GSTR-3B, and local officers have no discretionary power to waive these system-imposed late fees and interest.
Delayed scrutiny (issuing notices 3 to 4 years after filing) can create large accumulations of 18% annual interest and penalties for unintentional errors.
Issue scrutiny notices in the initial months rather than waiting 3 to 4 years, to avoid accumulation of interest and penalties for unintentional errors.
Build tighter systemic ITC validation to stop fake ITC generation at the source rather than relying solely on post-facto scrutiny.
The department identifies timely processing of queries and refund claims well before statutory deadlines, and early scrutiny rather than delaying notices for years, as a practice.
The department guides and trains taxpayers who want to file returns themselves, although officials do not file on their behalf.
Some agencies insist on a GST registration number for government schemes or bank loans, leading some people to register without taxable turnover, not file returns, and later face penalties.

Automated discrepancy detection flags a mismatch between GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B liability, or an ITC mismatch between a taxpayer's claim and supplier-declared data, triggering an online notice from the jurisdictional officer.
GST processes are broadly all-India in nature, with nothing Nagaland-specific described in the filing process.
Businesses must maintain books of accounts for 60 months under Sections 35 and 36, as cited by the expert.

gaps.text: No departmental resolution timeline for flagged discrepancies/online notices was mentioned by the expert.
Deemed approval for GST Tax Filing itself was not addressed; the expert referenced deemed approval only for GST registration, a separate service.
The department reportedly processes queries and refund claims well before statutory deadlines and pursues early scrutiny rather than delaying notices for years.
GST 2.0 reforms (effective 25 September 2025) were cited as having eased the filing process, though the expert did not specify exactly what changed.
No quantification of how often delayed scrutiny (3 to 4 years) actually occurs or its scale across Nagaland taxpayers was provided.
No application or statutory filing fee amount was explicitly confirmed; only late fees and interest for delayed filing/payment were described.
